lead: Bag of visual words (BoVW) describes an image by which local features it contains and how many of each, and ignores where they sit. Take SIFT descriptors from many training images, cluster them into k groups with k-means, and call each cluster centre a visual word. Any image then becomes a histogram of length k. Classifiers need fixed-length inputs and images give different numbers of descriptors, so this step is needed. BoVW powered image search and scene classification before deep learning, and it is still a fast baseline.
prereq: You need: 5.2 Feature descriptors: SIFT and SURF for the local descriptors, and basic k-means plus a standard classifier such as k-NN or SVM (see Unit 6, Recognition and Deep Learning for Vision).

blocks.text: A SIFT descriptor is a list of 128 numbers describing one small patch around a keypoint. One image gives a few hundred such vectors, and the count changes with image size, texture and the detector threshold. A classifier such as an SVM needs the same number of inputs for every image. BoVW turns the whole set into one vector of fixed length k.

The method borrows an idea from text search. A document is a bag of words when we count its words and ignore their order. Here each descriptor plays the role of a word, and the vocabulary of words is learned once from training images.

items: Collect SIFT or SURF descriptors from a large set of training images. Keep only the vectors, not their positions.
Choose k, the number of visual words. A few hundred to a few thousand is typical.
Run k-means on the descriptors: start with k centres, assign each descriptor to the nearest centre, move each centre to the mean of its assigned descriptors, repeat until the centres stop moving.
Store the k final centres. Each centre is one visual word; the set of centres is the vocabulary.

blocks.where: x is one descriptor vector (128 numbers for SIFT); C<sub>j</sub> is the set of descriptors assigned to word j; μ<sub>j</sub> is the centre of word j; ‖·‖ is Euclidean length; J is the total squared error that k-means shrinks.

blocks.text: The vocabulary is built once, offline, from training images. Every later image, training or test, is described with this same frozen vocabulary.

sections.h3: Assigning words and building the histogram

blocks.text: To describe a new image, detect keypoints as in 5.1, compute one descriptor per keypoint, and assign each descriptor to the nearest word by Euclidean distance. Then count how many descriptors fell on each word.

blocks.where: h<sub>i</sub> is the i-th entry of the histogram; n<sub>i</sub> is the number of descriptors assigned to word i; N is the total number of descriptors in the image. The entries sum to 1.

blocks.text: The vector [h<sub>1</sub>, h<sub>2</sub>, …, h<sub>k</sub>] is the image's BoVW feature. Its length is always k, whatever the image size. A classifier such as k-NN or an SVM is then trained on these vectors (Unit 6).

The numbering of words is arbitrary: word 1 may be a patch of grass and word 3 a patch of window. It must not change after training, because the classifier learns one weight per histogram position. A zero entry is not a missing value; it only means the image used no descriptor of that word.

sections.h3: Weighting, layout and a compact variant

blocks.text: Some words are useless. If a texture appears in almost every training image, its histogram entry is large everywhere and separates nothing. Text search solved this with tf-idf weighting, and BoVW borrows it:

blocks.where: n<sub>i</sub>/N is the term frequency of word i in this image; df<sub>i</sub> is the number of training images that contain word i at least once; N<sub>img</sub> is the total number of training images; w<sub>i</sub> is the weighted entry. A word found in every image gets log(1) = 0, so it is switched off.

blocks.text: The plain histogram throws away position. Spatial pyramid matching puts coarse position back: split the image into 1×1, 2×2 and 4×4 grids, build one histogram per cell, and concatenate them. That gives (1 + 4 + 16)k numbers, with the levels often weighted 1/4, 1/4 and 1/2.
VLAD is a compact extension that keeps more than counts. For each word, add up the residuals of the descriptors assigned to it:

blocks.where: x → i means x is a descriptor whose nearest word is i; μ<sub>i</sub> is that word's centre; v<sub>i</sub> is the summed residual for word i. The k blocks are concatenated into a vector of length k·d (d = 128 for SIFT) and L2-normalised.

examples.question: A vocabulary has k = 3 visual words. One image gives six SIFT descriptors, which are assigned to words [1, 1, 2, 3, 3, 3]. (a) Count the descriptors per word. (b) Build the normalised BoVW histogram. (c) Word 2 occurs in 400 of the 1000 training images. Using log base 10, find its tf-idf weight.
steps: Count the assignments: word 1 appears at positions 1 and 2, word 2 at position 3, word 3 at positions 4, 5 and 6. So n₁ = 2, n₂ = 1, n₃ = 3.
Divide each count by N: h₁ = 2/6 = 0.333, h₂ = 1/6 = 0.167, h₃ = 3/6 = 0.500. The histogram is [0.333, 0.167, 0.500] and sums to 1.000.
Term frequency of word 2: tf = n₂/N = 1/6 = 0.167.
Inverse document frequency: idf = log₁₀(N<sub>img</sub> / df₂) = log₁₀(1000/400) = log₁₀(2.5) = 0.398.
examples.answer: The normalised histogram is [0.333, 0.167, 0.500], and the tf-idf weight of word 2 is 0.066.
examples.check:
import math
assign = [1, 1, 2, 3, 3, 3]
k = 3
N = len(assign)
counts = [assign.count(w) for w in range(1, k + 1)]
print("counts:", counts)
print("total:", N)
hist = [round(c / N, 3) for c in counts]
print("histogram:", hist)
tf = 1 / N
idf = math.log10(1000 / 400)
print("tf:", round(tf, 3))
print("idf:", round(idf, 3))
print("tfidf:", round(tf * idf, 3))

traps: Re-running k-means on each test image. The word numbers change, so the new histogram cannot be compared with the training histograms. Fit the vocabulary once and freeze it.
Believing BoVW keeps layout. The histogram is blind to position; only a spatial pyramid adds coarse geometry.
Comparing histograms built from two different vocabularies, or training on raw counts and testing on unit-sum histograms. Use one vocabulary and one normalisation everywhere.
Mixing up the vocabulary size k with the descriptor length d. SIFT has d = 128 numbers per descriptor, while k is the number of words and the histogram length.
Treating the order of words as meaningful across runs. Two correct k-means runs may swap word 1 and word 3; only the pairing of vocabulary and histogram matters.

quiz.q: Define a visual word in one line.
quiz.a: A cluster centre in descriptor space, produced by k-means on training descriptors; it acts as a prototype patch that descriptors are matched against.

quiz.q: Why can the raw SIFT descriptors of an image not be fed straight to an SVM as one feature vector?
quiz.a: The number of descriptors per image varies with size and texture, while an SVM needs a fixed-length input. BoVW converts any image into a vector of length k.

quiz.q: A vocabulary has k = 4 words. An image's descriptors are assigned with counts n = [3, 0, 5, 2]. Build the normalised histogram.
A word has term frequency tf = 0.5 and appears in 100 of 1000 training images. Find its tf-idf weight using log base 10.
A photo of a beach and a photo of the same beach with a small boat give almost identical BoVW histograms. Explain why, and give one fix.
quiz.a: The boat covers a small area and adds only a few descriptors, so its histogram entries are tiny, and the plain histogram ignores where they are. A spatial pyramid over 1×1, 2×2 and 4×4 cells separates the two images because the boat's words land in particular cells.

quiz.q: A classmate says the vocabulary can be recomputed per test image for better accuracy. Argue against this.
quiz.a: k-means returns an arbitrary numbering of centres, so a fresh vocabulary gives a completely different histogram layout. The trained classifier's weights per position would then mean nothing, and histograms of different images could not be compared. The vocabulary must be fitted on training data and frozen.

quiz.q: What does tf-idf do to a word that appears in every training image, and why is that useful?
quiz.a: It gives that word idf = log(1) = 0, so its entry carries no weight. Such words (flat sky, plain wall) are common everywhere and do not help separate classes.

beyond: Not for the exam. Fisher vectors and VLAD with power and L2 normalisation gave the strongest results in pre-deep-learning image retrieval, and large vocabularies needed approximate nearest neighbour search to stay fast. Deep CNN features have since replaced hand-crafted descriptors for most recognition tasks, but BoVW-style pooling of CNN activations still appears in some retrieval pipelines. Search next for spatial pyramid matching, VLAD, Fisher vector, and inverted file indexing for large vocabularies.
